label: Grain bins, hoppers and silos
summary: Flowing grain acts like quicksand: someone standing on grain while a bin empties is trapped in about 5 seconds and covered in as little as 11 to 22 seconds, and crusted grain can collapse under or onto you with nothing running. Bins and silos can also hold silo gas or air with no oxygen, grain dust explodes, and augers and conveyors can catch you. Would-be rescuers often die too.
signs: Steel grain bins, hopper bins, silos, elevators and feed mills, and wagons or trucks full of grain
Augers and conveyors at the base, and unloading or sweep augers inside: anything that could start while someone is in or on the grain
Crusted, clumped or mouldy grain, grain stuck high on the walls, or a top with no funnel in the middle after some has been drawn out: the grain has bridged over a hollow
Silage silos after filling: a bleach smell or a yellow, red or brown haze at the top, down the chute or in the feed room means silo gas. It may have no smell at all
Sealed oxygen-limiting silos, built of bolted glass-fused-to-steel panels with breather bags inside: they fill with carbon dioxide and the air in them can't keep you alive

Pellets or 'ropes' in or on stored grain, or plates, pouches or strips in an empty bin: phosphine fumigant, a poison gas heavier than air that smells of fish or garlic, though pure phosphine has no smell
Grain dust on floors, ledges and around bucket elevators, grinders and dryers: even 3 mm (1/8 in) is enough to fuel a fire or explosion
do: Stay out of bins if you can: check the grain from the hatch, and knock down crusts and hang-ups from outside with a long pole through a hatch or access door
Before anyone goes in, shut off, disconnect and lock out every auger and conveyor so nothing can start; whoever goes in keeps the key
Enter only in a full-body harness on a lifeline anchored outside and kept short enough that you can't sink past your waist, with one person at the hatch watching and another on the ground
Test the air at the hatch and ventilate before going in; in a silo, keep the blower running while you're inside
If grain stuck to the walls has to be cleaned off, work from top to bottom, in a harness on a lifeline, with the augers locked off and a person outside watching
If the grain starts to flow, move to the outer wall and keep walking
If you find phosphine pellets, ropes, plates, pouches or strips in a bin, keep out of it: NIOSH rates 50 ppm of phosphine as immediately dangerous to life, and pure phosphine has no smell
dont: Don't go into a bin, hopper, wagon or truck while grain is being drawn out or anything could start: the flow pulls you under in seconds
Don't walk on grain to make it flow, and don't stand on a crust, under a bridge or beside a steep wall of grain
Don't go in alone, and don't go in after a buried or collapsed person: bin accidents often kill the would-be rescuers too. Stop the augers and work from outside

Stay out of a silo after filling: Ontario says the air stays unfit for up to 2 weeks and keeps visitors away for 3, OSHA says not for 4 to 6 weeks and even then it may not be safe. Silo gas spills down the chute into the feed room: ventilate it. Never enter a sealed oxygen-limiting silo
Don't weld, grind or cut near grain dust, and keep dust off hot bearings, motors and belts
Don't work near an exposed auger, belt or conveyor while it can start: they can catch you
ppe: A full-body harness and lifeline tied off outside the bin (see Fall from height for harness limits)
A respirator for grain and mould dust: an N95 or better that seals on a shaven face; Alberta's farm guide calls for an approved toxic-dust respirator
No filter mask helps against silo gas or oxygen-poor air: that takes air-supplied breathing apparatus
firstAid: Someone sinking or buried: stop every auger and conveyor at once, and keep their lifeline taut so they sink no further

Pulling by hand rarely works: someone stuck to the waist needs about twice their body weight in pull, and 30 cm (1 ft) of grain over a person weighs about 136 kg (300 lb). Freeing them takes a winch or rescue gear and a team
Collapsed in a silo or bin from gas: start the blower at once and pull them out from outside on the lifeline; don't go in
Once they're out, check breathing and start CPR if they aren't breathing normally (see Confined spaces: pits, tanks, wells, silos)
After silo gas, a cough or breathlessness can start or worsen hours later: keep them resting and watched; they need medical care
